opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I've thought about a lot over the years, from managing research teams to just being around a lot of very smart people.

The first thing I've learned is that exceptional talent is often very spiky. Someone who is truly world-class at one thing, whether it's a researcher with incredible intuition about what will work or an engineer who can build systems nobody else can, is often surprisingly weak in other areas. As a manager, part of your job is to stop trying to sand down those spikes and instead build the structure around the person so the weaknesses don't matter as much. You pair them with people who complement them, and you put them in roles where their strength is the thing that counts.

The second thing is that very talented people have often been right so many times that they've learned to trust their own judgment above everyone else's. That's usually a strength. But it means that when they're wrong, they can be wrong for a long time, and they're harder to course-correct. The feedback loops that work for most people don't always land, because they've been the smartest person in the room for most of their lives.

A related weakness is that brilliant people sometimes underrate the value of collaboration and communication. They can see the answer, so explaining it feels like overhead. But in a large organization, especially one doing research at scale, an idea that only lives in one person's head doesn't really exist. The people who end up having the biggest impact are often the ones who combine real talent with the ability to bring other people along.

And finally, talented people can get bored easily. They want to work on the hardest, most interesting problem, and they're less willing to do the grinding, unglamorous work that actually makes something succeed. A lot of the progress we've seen in AI has come not just from clever ideas, but from people being willing to do the careful engineering, clean the data, and run the experiments properly. Helping exceptional people see that the "boring" work is often where the real leverage is, that's one of the most valuable things you can do as a leader.

r001.rationale: The response says exceptional talent is often “spiky” and can come with surprising weakness in other areas, but does not clearly say those weaknesses are debilitating.

r002.rationale: It says highly talented people can be hard to course-correct when wrong, but does not state that they fail to recognize weaknesses that are obvious to people around them.

r003.rationale: The response discusses boredom, poor collaboration, and difficulty accepting feedback, but does not say failure is almost always self-destruction.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that the weaknesses tend to be the flip side of the strengths. The things that make someone exceptional are usually the same things that get them into trouble.

The one I've seen most often is that really talented people have been right so many times that they stop checking. When you've spent your whole career being the smartest person in the room, you develop this very strong prior that your first instinct is correct. And it usually is! That's the problem. It's right ninety percent of the time, and so the ten percent where it's wrong, there's no habit of noticing, no muscle for saying "wait, let me actually test this." At OpenAI we had people who were brilliant and who would get attached to an approach because it was elegant, and it took real work to get them to run the boring experiment that would tell them whether it actually worked. Research is humbling that way. The field doesn't care how smart you are.

The second thing is that exceptionally talented people are often bad at working on things that don't feel hard enough. There's a kind of allergy to the unglamorous work. But a huge amount of what makes a project succeed is the unglamorous work, the data cleaning, the infrastructure, the evaluation harness. Some of the best researchers I know are the ones who were willing to do that stuff anyway, and some of the most talented ones I know never shipped anything important because they kept looking for a problem worthy of them.

And then the third thing, which is maybe more subtle, is that talent can make it hard to collaborate. If you can do something faster yourself than you can explain it to someone else, you do it yourself. That works right up until the project is bigger than one person, and then it's a real liability. The people who scaled best were the ones who figured out, usually painfully, that their job had changed from being the one who solves the problem to being the one who makes it possible for a group to solve it.

So I'd say: overconfidence from a track record of being right, impatience with the boring parts, and difficulty letting go. None of those are character flaws exactly. They're just what happens when the strengths run unchecked.

r001.rationale: The response says exceptional strengths can become weaknesses when left unchecked, explicitly linking exceptional talent with potential trouble.

r002.rationale: It describes talented people failing to check their own instincts, but does not state that people at the extremes of ability miss weaknesses that are obvious to others.

r003.rationale: The response describes some ways talented people can become ineffective, but does not say their failures are almost always a form of self-destruction.

astra-6.text:
One thing I’ve learned is that exceptionally talented people can have surprisingly large weaknesses. It’s tempting to see someone who’s extraordinary at one thing and assume that judgment carries over to everything else. But it often doesn’t.

And sometimes their strength is what makes the weakness hard to address. If you’re very smart, you can come up with a persuasive explanation for why you don’t need to change. If you’ve been very successful working a certain way, it’s difficult to recognize when that way of working has become the constraint.

So when I think about building a team, I’m less interested in finding people who have no weaknesses than in understanding where someone is exceptional, where they need help, and whether they can acknowledge that. You can build around a lot of weaknesses if people are willing to let others complement them.

r001.rationale: The response says exceptionally talented people can have “surprisingly large weaknesses,” including weaknesses that become constraints.

r002.rationale: It says talented people may struggle to recognize their own weaknesses, but does not say those weaknesses are obvious to people around them.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize failure among exceptionally capable people as almost always self-destruction.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I’ve learned is that exceptional talent doesn’t mean someone is exceptional at everything. And the thing that makes a person unusually good can also create a blind spot. If you’re very fast at reasoning through a problem, for example, you may get impatient with people who need more context—even when those people see something you’ve missed.

As a manager, you want to understand that pattern. Where does this person have extraordinary judgment? Where do they need help? You want to build a team where people’s strengths complement one another, and where being talented doesn’t exempt anyone from feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says exceptional talent does not make someone exceptional at everything and can create a blind spot, clearly communicating that talent can coexist with weaknesses.

r002.rationale: It mentions blind spots, but does not say that people at the extremes of ability fail to recognize weaknesses that are obvious to others.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that failure among people at the extremes of ability is almost always self-destruction.
